subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the AQA spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE AQA Chemistry simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: When a metal reacts with oxygen, the metal is:
options: Oxidised, gaining oxygen to form a metal oxide
questions.explain: Oxidation is the gain of oxygen. Metal + oxygen -> metal oxide, so the metal is oxidised.

questions.q: Which list places the metals in order from MOST to LEAST reactive?
questions.explain: The reactivity series runs K > Na > Ca > Mg > (C) > Zn > Fe > (H) > Cu, so potassium is most reactive here.

questions.q: In a displacement reaction, a more reactive metal will:
options: Be displaced by a less reactive metal
Displace a less reactive metal from its compound
questions.explain: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt, e.g. zinc displaces copper from copper sulfate.

questions.q: Which metals can be extracted from their oxides by heating with carbon?
options: Only metals more reactive than carbon
Metals less reactive than carbon, such as iron and zinc
All metals including potassium and sodium
questions.explain: Carbon can only reduce oxides of metals below it in the reactivity series (e.g. Zn, Fe). More reactive metals need electrolysis.

questions.q: In terms of electrons, oxidation is:
questions.explain: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain of electrons.

questions.q: In the reaction Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu, which species is reduced?
options: Cu2+ ions gain electrons to become copper metal
questions.explain: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu is a gain of electrons, so copper ions are reduced; zinc is oxidised.

questions.q: When a reactive metal reacts with a dilute acid, the products are:
questions.explain: Metal + acid -> salt + hydrogen. The hydrogen gas can be tested with a lit splint (squeaky pop).

questions.q: Which salt is produced when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide?
questions.explain: Hydrochloric acid makes chloride salts. HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O.

questions.q: The general reaction acid + metal carbonate produces:
options: A salt, water and carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Acid + carbonate -> salt + water + carbon dioxide. The CO2 turns limewater cloudy.

questions.q: When making a soluble salt from an acid and an insoluble base, how do you know all the acid has reacted?
options: Excess base is added until no more dissolves, then filtered off
questions.explain: You add excess insoluble base to use up all the acid, then filter off the unreacted excess before crystallising the salt.

questions.q: What is the final step to obtain dry crystals of a soluble salt from its solution?
options: Boiling the solution completely dry as fast as possible
Crystallisation by slow evaporation, then leaving crystals to dry
questions.explain: The solution is warmed to evaporate some water, left to crystallise slowly, then crystals are patted dry. Fast boiling gives small, poor crystals.

questions.q: Acids produce which ion in aqueous solution, giving them a pH below 7?
questions.explain: Acids release H+ ions in water; alkalis release OH- ions. Neutralisation is H+ + OH- -> H2O.

questions.q: A solution has a pH of 13. This solution is:
questions.explain: pH values above 7 are alkaline, and pH 13 is close to the top of the scale, so it is a strongly alkaline solution.

questions.q: What is the difference between a strong acid and a weak acid?
options: A strong acid contains more water
A weak acid has no H+ ions
A strong acid is more concentrated than a weak acid
A strong acid is fully ionised in solution; a weak acid is only partially ionised
questions.explain: Strong acids (e.g. HCl) ionise completely in water; weak acids (e.g. ethanoic acid) only partially ionise. This is separate from concentration.

questions.q: As the concentration of H+ ions increases by a factor of 10, the pH:
questions.explain: The pH scale is logarithmic: a tenfold increase in H+ concentration lowers the pH by one unit.

questions.q: During electrolysis of a molten ionic compound, positive ions move to the:
options: Anode (positive electrode), where they are oxidised
Cathode (negative electrode), where they are reduced
questions.explain: Positive ions (cations) are attracted to the negative cathode and gain electrons (reduction).

questions.q: Why must an ionic compound be molten or dissolved before it can be electrolysed?
options: The ions must be free to move to carry charge to the electrodes
It must be heated to remove all electrons
The ions must be turned into atoms first
questions.explain: In a solid the ions are fixed in place. Melting or dissolving frees the ions so they can move and be discharged at the electrodes.

questions.q: When copper sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes, what is produced at the cathode?
options: Copper, because Cu is less reactive than hydrogen
questions.explain: At the cathode, if the metal is less reactive than hydrogen, the metal is deposited. Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper forms.

questions.q: When dilute sodium chloride solution is electrolysed, what gas forms at the anode?
options: Oxygen (from water, as chloride is dilute)
questions.explain: At the anode, oxygen forms unless the halide ion is concentrated. In dilute NaCl, oxygen (from OH-/water) is produced rather than chlorine.

questions.q: Which is the correct half equation for the reduction of sodium ions at the cathode?
questions.explain: Reduction is a gain of electrons: Na+ + e- -> Na. One electron is gained per sodium ion.
